verses.1: Al-Mizan presents this sūrah as a warning (indhār): God’s custom (sunnah ilāhiyyah) is to send prophets and reminders despite people’s excesses, then destroy persistent mockers before their enduring punishment. It chiefly repudiates the claim that God has offspring, especially that angels are His daughters; it appears Meccan, although the alleged exception at (43:45) is not established. Ḥā, Mīm and the Manifest Book introduce an oath whose answer is the Qur’an’s Arabic revelation. ‘Manifest’ (mubīn) may mean clarifying guidance or self-evidently free of doubt. The Arabic Qur’an makes intelligible a Book whose original reality is beyond conceptual, linguistic intellect: in the Mother Book, the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), it is sublime (ʿalī) and firm (ḥakīm), undivided and epistemically dense. What people read is its similitude (nisbat al-mithl wa al-mumaththal), not an intelligible grasp of that original state; this defeats readings that reduce those qualities to eloquence, superiority over other books, praise, or generic wisdom. The rhetorical question at (43:5) therefore asks whether their profligacy warrants withholding the Reminder; it does not. Earlier peoples likewise received prophets, mocked them, and were destroyed, promising support to the Prophet and warning his people. Their own admission that God creates all things proves that the Creator’s ordering of creation—including earth, routes, measured rain, and revival of dead land—belongs to Him alone and also establishes resurrection. The earth’s ‘cradle’ and routes primarily guide travel, not directly worship; creating and governing cannot be divided. Pairs encompass created kinds, and the ungoverned use of ‘ride’ for ships and beasts follows their juxtaposition. Transport is a divine blessing that calls for gratitude, not merely tasbīḥ and tanzīh: reports from the Prophet and the Imams of his Household include taḥmīd, and a report in Kashshāf from Ḥasan b. ʿAlī makes remembering the blessing, rather than only reciting the glorification, the command. Return to the Lord finally attests resurrection.

verses.3: Al-Mizan says that making the Manifest Book an Arabic Qur’an serves the end that people may understand it. This implies that its native reality lies beyond the human intellect, which only grasps concepts and ordered propositions. In the Mother Book (umm al-kitāb), identified with the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), the Book is ‘sublime’ (ʿalī), beyond human reach, and ‘firm’ (ḥakīm), that is, muḥkam and not yet divided into sūrahs, verses, sentences, or words. Its Arabic form therefore makes comprehensible what is otherwise suprarational. The apparent correspondence between the Qur’an in human hands and the Mother Book does not erase this distinction: their relation may be that of a similitude to what it represents (nisbat al-mithl wa al-mumaththal), which is identical to it while being all that its recipient understands. The commentary accordingly rejects explanations of ʿalī and ḥakīm as mere eloquence, abrogating superiority, praise, extreme wisdom, or a hyperbolic claim that the Qur’an’s statements are wise; they fail to reckon with its descent from the Mother Book.

verses.5: Al-Mizan takes the question as a rebuke: should God turn the Reminder aside merely because its hearers are a profligate people? ‘Strike’ (ḍarb) acquired the sense of turning aside, as Ṭabrisī reports in Majmaʿ al-Bayān from striking one side of a mount to divert it. Safḥ, literally turning away, states the motive: the question asks whether the Arabic Book should be withheld out of disregard for them.
verses.6: Al-Mizan reads ‘how many’ (kam) as a multitude and al-awwalūn as the known earlier peoples. Their continual derision of every prophet explains why present profligacy does not cause God to withhold revelation: His established way is to send guidance even to mockers, then destroy nations stronger than the present audience. The verses thus promise the Prophet divine support and threaten his people with the same outcome.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads ‘how many’ (kam) as a multitude and al-awwalūn as the known earlier peoples. Their continual derision of every prophet explains why present profligacy does not cause God to withhold revelation: His established way is to send guidance even to mockers, then destroy nations stronger than the present audience. The verses thus promise the Prophet divine support and threaten his people with the same outcome.
verses.8: Al-Mizan glosses baṭsh as forceful seizure. The move from addressing the audience to speaking of ‘these’ to the Prophet marks their refusal to heed the stories and prepares the next address to him. ‘The example of the ancients has passed’ means earlier Qur’anic sūrahs have related those nations and the fate that overtook the very derision they practised.
verses.9: Al-Mizan treats this as the introduction to a conclusive proof of God’s exclusive lordship (rubūbiyyah), completed through creation, providential ordering, and resurrection. The idolaters already acknowledged God as sole creator, but assigned the running of the world to others. The coming survey of earth, routes, rain, and the return to God exposes that separation as incoherent: the sole Creator is also sovereign organizer and sole Lord.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains the earth as a cradle in which people grow and its ways as routes to their destinations; the proposed reading that they guide directly to knowledge of God is less apparent. The renewed direct address emphasizes that creation and the world’s governance are one reality. Thus those who confess God’s sole creation yet ascribe management to other beings contradict themselves.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says measured rain displays deliberate provision, and the revival of a ‘dead’ land concerns a physical locale. The shift from third-person description to ‘We revived’ intensifies the point. Rain and vegetation prove both creation and divine governance, but also resurrection, without which divine unity is incomplete: as dead land is revived, people will be raised from their graves. Calling vegetation’s emergence ‘revival’ while calling human resurrection ‘bringing forth’ magnifies the former and makes the latter’s difficulty seem slight.
verses.12: Al-Mizan reports that ‘pairs’ may mean all created kinds or all opposites. It notes that rukūb takes no preposition with animals but ordinarily needs fī with a ship; its unqualified use here follows the coupling of ships with cattle. Sitting ‘on their backs’ means being settled on the conveyed thing. Remembering the Lord’s blessing is awareness of the benefit of transport and, apparently, thanksgiving to its giver, not merely the formula of tasbīḥ and tanzīh, which declares God free of partners. Reports from the Prophet and the Imams of his Household therefore add taḥmīd when mounting; a Kashshāf report from Ḥasan b. ʿAlī likewise corrects a rider who recites only the glorification by directing him to remember his Lord’s blessing.

verses.14: Al-Mizan reads turning toward the Lord as return to Him, and therefore as testimony to the resurrection.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains juzʾ, ‘offspring,’ literally as a separated part. Calling a child God’s part exposes the claim’s impossibility: taking a part presupposes a composite (murakkab) source, whereas God is absolutely and indivisibly one. ‘From among His servants’ clarifies the alleged part, even though it precedes the clause it explains.
verses.16: Al-Mizan says the question shames the idolaters for assigning God daughters while preferring sons for themselves, even though the attribution is already impossible. ‘From what He creates’ recalls that they themselves considered the angels created, despite their imagined lordship and divinity. The turn from ‘they’ to ‘you’ sharpens the rebuke, while the indefinite daughters and definite sons respectively belittle and aggrandize the two in their own value-system.
verses.17: Al-Mizan identifies the ‘like’ (mathal) as the female child they ascribe to the All-beneficent and kaẓīm as one full of anguish and anger. The verse exposes their contradiction: a man’s face darkens and he chokes with distress at news of a daughter, treating her as shameful, yet he is content to assign daughters to God. The shift back to third-person presents their ugly conduct to an outside observer for shock.
verses.18: Al-Mizan paraphrases the rebuke as asking whether they assign God one raised amid ornament and unable to state her case in contest. It says these two traits are mentioned because women, in its account, ordinarily have stronger emotion and empathy but less capacity for reason and logical argument than men, whose disposition is described as the reverse.
verses.19: Al-Mizan says some pre-Islamic Arabs claimed angels were God’s daughters, while other idolaters may have posited mother or daughter deities without claiming every angel female. Describing angels as servants of the All-beneficent refutes femininity, but does not make them male in the material sense: sex belongs to material procreation, from which angels are remote. Their claim lacks knowledge because they did not witness the angels’ creation. The rhetorical question therefore rebukes speech without knowledge and warns that their fabrication will be recorded and questioned on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.20: Al-Mizan reads their appeal to God’s will primarily as an attempted justification of worshipping the angels, rather than principally a denial of prophetic commands. They reason that because they worship associates, God did not will them not to do so and therefore approves it. The argument confuses creative will (al-irādah al-takwīniyyah) with moral will (al-irādah al-tashrīʿiyyah). God’s not preventing an act creatively means that humans act freely and may choose it; it neither entails His pleasure nor cancels His moral will that they believe in divine unity and abandon associates. The commentary faults the claim that absence of a will against something proves a will for it: at most it implies permission (idhn). It also rejects the reading that they admitted angel-worship was wrong, since their subsequent appeal to their fathers shows they considered it justified. Their kharṣ is conjectural assertion, or, on another interpretation, lying.
verses.21: Al-Mizan says this denies any revealed warrant for angel-worship just as the preceding verse denied it rational warrant. They possess neither scripture nor reason for it, and therefore no divine permission.
verses.22: Al-Mizan defines ummah here as a followed path, hence a religion (dīn). The adversative shows that, lacking rational and scriptural evidence, the idolaters rely only on finding their fathers upon a creed and blindly following them.
verses.23: Al-Mizan generalizes their ancestral imitation to earlier idolatrous towns: every warner faced affluent people who refused to leave their fathers’ religion. The special mention of the wealthy shows that wealth and ease prompt this blind adherence and prevent serious consideration of truth.
verses.24: Al-Mizan identifies the speaker as the earlier warner asking whether they would keep ancestral religion even if he brought better guidance. ‘Better’ is concessive argumentation, not an admission that their false religion contains guidance. Their reply—disbelief in what he was sent with—is arbitrary rejection without proof.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says that after a warner challenged ancestral imitation and was denied, God destroyed those earlier peoples. The command to observe their fate warns the Prophet’s own people of that consequence.
verses.26: Al-Mizan notes that barāʾun, ‘I repudiate,’ is a verbal noun used hyperbolically: Abraham is presented as repudiation itself, not merely one who repudiates. He renounced everything his father and people worshipped besides God, idols and heavenly bodies alike. In context this contrasts his reflection on truth with their unreasoned imitation of their fathers after he had challenged their idolatry.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says Abraham excepts God, who originated him (fiṭr), and this origination proves God’s exclusive lordship: bringing beings into existence is inseparable from managing their affairs, so their Originator alone deserves worship. ‘He will guide me’ primarily means guidance to the truth Abraham seeks, though it is also said to mean the road to Paradise. Guidance toward perfection is itself a necessary work of lordship, so worshipping God in unity entails divine guidance. The exception is disjunctive, since idolaters do not truly worship God; the conjunctive reading is reported but not adopted.
verses.28: Al-Mizan takes God as the maker of Abraham’s repudiating word, the same in meaning as the profession of divine unity, a lasting word among his descendants. It does not mean a negation of all gods followed by an affirmation, but negates every alleged god other than God. Its endurance means that monotheists will always remain among Abraham’s progeny, so that idolaters among them may return to sole worship; this may answer Abraham’s prayer at (14:35). The reading that Abraham himself made it lasting merely by enjoining it on his children is inadequate to ‘making’ it enduring. A reported reading makes the enduring word the Imamate, but the apparent sense is that this word endures among his descendants until the Resurrection.
verses.29: Al-Mizan says ‘rather’ reverses the hoped-for return to divine unity: God supplied these people and their fathers with blessings until the truth—the Qur’an—and the manifest Messenger, Muḥammad, came. The first-person singular stresses the magnitude of their ingratitude, disbelief, and later charge of sorcery, which are in reality directed against God Himself.
verses.30: Al-Mizan says their calling the Qur’an magic imputes the truth itself and necessarily the Messenger who brought it. The same implication lies in their ensuing question why the Qur’an was not sent to someone else.
verses.31: Al-Mizan identifies the two cities as Mecca and Ṭāʾif and ‘great’ as worldly wealth and rank. The objectors assume prophethood must belong to an eminent, powerful notable and therefore disparage the Prophet as lacking such standing. Majmaʿ al-Bayān reports various named candidates from Qatādah, Mujāhid, and Ibn ʿAbbās, but the commentary regards these as applications: the objection was general while likely imagining one grandee from either city.
verses.32: Al-Mizan identifies the Lord’s mercy (raḥmah) here as prophethood (nubuwwah). The rebuke asks how people who do not even control the distribution of their temporary livelihoods can claim authority over the greater mercy that leads to eternal happiness. Wealth, health, children, and every sought provision demonstrate divine apportionment: human will and action are only incomplete causes (asbāb nāqiṣah), dependent on innumerable causes held by God. Status too depends on God-given traits, wealth, and circumstances. The elevation of some above others may also explain social interdependence: diverse needs, unequal surplus, exchange, labour, and mutual use make people serve and be served. None of this makes worldly accumulation comparable to prophethood, which is better than what they amass.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says that even silver roofs, stairways, doors, couches, and ornaments for the faithless would show the world’s goods to have no intrinsic worth. One reading is that God withholds this lest all people disbelieve when they see unbelievers richly adorned and believers deprived. Another makes ‘one community’ equality in access to worldly means regardless of belief. In either case, these ornaments are fleeting wares. The Hereafter mentioned as ‘life’ is the felicitous Hereafter alone, for wretched afterlife is not truly life, and it is reserved by God’s decree for the Godwary; this supports the first reading.

verses.36: Al-Mizan says yaʿshu is feigned blindness, not an actual defect. Whoever deliberately disregards the remembrance of the All-beneficent—called remembrance of the All-beneficent to show that dhikr is mercy—is assigned a devil as an inseparable companion. This begins the contrary fate to that of the Godwary: turning from the truth yields companionship, misguidance, and ultimately punishment with that devil.
verses.37: Al-Mizan takes the first ‘they’ as the companion devils and the later pronouns as those who turned from God’s remembrance. The devils divert them from the way of divine unity while they suppose themselves guided. A person’s original fiṭrah inclines to truth, but persistent preference for desire after truth is presented brings sealing of the heart, blindness, and satanic wilāyah; falsehood then appears to be truth. The worldly veil will be removed at resurrection, as (18:101–104) and (50:22–27) describe.
verses.38: Al-Mizan says the companion devils continue their work until each heedless person comes to God at resurrection. Mashriqayn, literally ‘the two easts,’ abbreviates east and west. When error and its punishment become plain, the person wishes the devil were as far away as east from west and calls it an evil companion. Their continued company is itself an additional punishment, which is why it commands attention above the other torments.
verses.39: Al-Mizan most plausibly joins this to the preceding state: on Judgement Day, those who corrupted others and their companion devils share punishment, but that sharing gives no consolation because the companions’ presence is itself further torment. It rejects readings that make the verse only say their common punishment is undiminished, or that shared pain cannot be lightened as worldly hardship can; neither fits the stated reason that sharing is of no avail. A different reading tying it to the wish for separation fails because its two proposed explanations of that failure do not cohere.
verses.40: Al-Mizan says that, after describing people so blinded by satanic companionship that error appears guidance, God rhetorically tells the Prophet he cannot make such deaf hear or such blind find the way. He should neither exhaust himself inviting them nor grieve at their turning away.
verses.41: Al-Mizan says that whether God takes the Prophet away before vengeance or lets him see the promised vengeance while present, it is certain and within God’s encompassing power. ‘Taking away’ is reported to mean death, or removal from among them; the emphatic form confirms that neither possibility prevents retribution.
verses.42: Al-Mizan says that whether God takes the Prophet away before vengeance or lets him see the promised vengeance while present, it is certain and within God’s encompassing power. ‘Taking away’ is reported to mean death, or removal from among them; the emphatic form confirms that neither possibility prevents retribution.
verses.43: Al-Mizan makes this command the conclusion of the preceding argument: revelation follows the divine custom, the revealed Book and its manifest Messenger are true, only the Godwary answer, satanic companions turn the rest away, and their belief or disbelief brings the Prophet no gain while God will take vengeance. He is therefore to hold fast to revelation, for he is on the straight path.
verses.44: Al-Mizan prefers dhikr here as God’s remembrance, a recurring theme of the sūrah. ‘For you and your people’ specifies that its duties address them, as the coming questioning at resurrection confirms. It notes the common alternative that dhikr means the honour bestowed on the Prophet and Arabs by being remembered through the Qur’an.
verses.45: Al-Mizan rejects the interpretations that command asking earlier communities or the People of the Two Books about their messengers, especially the latter’s unexplained restriction. It reports instead that the command belongs to the Night Ascension, when the Prophet was to ask the gathered spirits of earlier prophets whether they had brought anything other than divine unity. More than one narration from the Imams of the Prophet’s Household supports this reading, to be treated in the narration discussion.
verses.46: Al-Mizan notes that laqad carries an oath and bi- in ‘with Our signs’ accompaniment. Moses was sent with God’s signs to Pharaoh and his elite as Messenger of the Lord of all worlds.
verses.47: Al-Mizan says Moses’ signs were miracles proving his messengership, while Pharaoh’s people laughed in derision and disparagement of them.
verses.48: Al-Mizan reads each sign as ‘greater than its sister,’ meaning each was an irrefutable proof of Moses’ truth, despite their laughter. The punishments were the plagues—drought, crop failure, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—sent so that they might abandon arrogance and return.
verses.49: Al-Mizan says the covenant is variously reported as relief from punishment upon belief or a promise to answer Moses’ prayer. ‘O magician’ and ‘your Lord’ are, in its view, arrogant mockery, not the alleged Egyptian honorific for a scholar; they ask only for relief and promise guidance in return.
verses.50: Al-Mizan glosses nakth as breaking a pledge: once the punishment was lifted, they violated their promise that they would be guided.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains Pharaoh’s proclamation as a public call among his people. His rivers are the Nile channels flowing beneath his palace or gardens; the grammatical alternatives do not change his boast that Egypt and its flowing rivers belong to him. ‘Do you not perceive?’ recalls that boast for their assent.
verses.52: Al-Mizan says Pharaoh calls Moses lowly because of his visible poverty and dishevelment, and alleges unclear speech, perhaps referring to Moses before God removed his impediment. The grammatical readings of am either make him affirm his superiority or ask it rhetorically; the reported linkage to ‘Do you not perceive?’ makes his superiority the consequence of their supposed insight. In all cases, omitting Moses’ name and calling him unable to speak are devices of belittlement.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains aswirah as bracelets and reports that leaders were adorned with gold; Pharaoh therefore treats material regalia as proof of leadership. His demand for accompanying angels invokes iqtirān in the sense of mutual accompaniment, asking angels to attest Moses’ prophethood, an argument repeatedly made by deniers of messengers.
verses.54: Al-Mizan reads Pharaoh’s carrying away of his people as carrying away their intellects and sound judgment; their obedience manifests their transgression.
verses.55: Al-Mizan says rousing divine wrath means provoking God’s will to punish. Their profligacy brought vengeance, and all were drowned.
verses.56: Al-Mizan takes salaf, the vanguard, to mean Pharaoh’s people precede others into hell, and mathal to mean they become a proverbial lesson for later people who reflect on their story.
verses.57: Al-Mizan’s contextual reading takes the cited example of Jesus to evoke the Meccan Sūrah Maryam and its account of God’s blessings on prophets. Quraysh respond with noise and mockery—or, on the alternate reading, turning away—and treat the Christian claim that Jesus is divine as though it could rank their gods against him. Their question is not inquiry but contentiousness, and their refusal to engage the Qur’an’s own description of Jesus exposes its futility.

verses.59: Al-Mizan holds that Jesus was a worshipping servant, blessed with prophethood, the Holy Spirit, and miracles, and made an extraordinary divine sign for the Children of Israel; he was not a god whose divinity could be compared with idols. It rejects as unreliable (ḍaʿīf), even baseless according to Ibn Ḥajar, the Ibn al-Zabʿarī report connecting the verses to (21:98), citing its inconsistencies and poor fit. It likewise rejects interpretations tied to the Medinan (3:59), or readings that make their comparison a defense of worshipping angels, because they disconnect the following description of Jesus. A narration from ʿAlī likens his place in the ummah to Jesus—ruinous excess in love, ruinous excess in hatred, and salvation in moderation—but does not itself explain ‘our gods or he’; if it prompted the verse, the objection concerns following ʿAlī’s guardianship. The verse itself refutes the premise by defining Jesus as God’s blessed servant and sign.
verses.60: Al-Mizan connects this to the claim that a human could not receive Jesus’ perfections and miraculous powers without becoming divine. God can purify a human until his heart is angelic while he remains a human servant living and succeeding on earth, so angel-like acts do not make Jesus a lord. It rejects the alternative that God would destroy humans and replace them with angels, since that does not fit the section.
verses.61: Al-Mizan identifies ‘he’ as Jesus and ʿilm as that by which something is known: his fatherless creation and raising of the dead show that the Hour is possible, so it must not be doubted. The readings that make him a future sign through descent, or make the pronoun the Qur’an, do not explain the prohibition on doubt. ‘Follow Me’ is reported either as God’s call to His guidance, religion, or Messenger, or as speech God orders the Prophet to say.
verses.62: Al-Mizan glosses ṣadd as turning aside and calls Satan the manifest enemy who must not bar people from the way.
verses.63: Al-Mizan identifies Jesus’ manifest proofs as miracles and his wisdom as revealed true belief and virtuous character. ‘Some of what you differ about’ most naturally concerns disputed legal deeds and affairs, since wisdom has already been mentioned, although beliefs are not impossible. It rejects unrestricted or merely worldly-religious alternatives for lack of support. Jesus’ command to fear God and obey him confirms that he claims messengership, not divinity.
verses.64: Al-Mizan says Jesus summons people to worship God alone as both his Lord and theirs. This is a conclusive argument against attributing divinity to him.
verses.65: Al-Mizan divides Jesus’ community into those who disbelieved, believers who exaggerated (ghuluw), and believers who remained moderate. The warning of a painful day reaches both extremes: denying him and holding him divine.
verses.66: Al-Mizan distinguishes the Hour’s sudden arrival from their unawareness: they are heedless because absorbed in worldly affairs. Their condition is that of people warned of destruction who do nothing to escape it, thereby displaying indifference to belief and salvation.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains akhillāʾ as friends who compensate each other’s need. Every friendship and affection not for God’s countenance becomes mutual help toward eternal misery and turns to enmity; friendship among the Godwary instead endures and benefits them. A prophetic report says all worldly relations and brotherhood disappear at resurrection except brotherhood for God’s sake.
verses.68: Al-Mizan takes this as God’s speech to His servants on the Day of Resurrection. Removing fear removes dread of a possible harm, and removing grief removes distress at an assured harm; together they guarantee safety from every unpleasantness.
verses.69: Al-Mizan takes this as either apposition to, or an adjective of, God’s servants. His signs include every pointer to God—prophet, scripture, or otherwise—and muslims are those who submit to His will and obey His command.
verses.70: Al-Mizan says the spouses are believing women of this world, since the ḥūr al-ʿīn are already in Paradise rather than entering with them. Tuḥbarūn denotes happiness visible on the face, or splendid adornment; the command promises entry with faithful wives in manifest delight.
verses.71: Al-Mizan reads the golden dishes and handleless goblets as food and drink. The shift to third-person service magnifies the honor promised directly to the believers. What souls desire includes bodily pleasures, while what eyes delight in denotes splendor and beauty, perhaps also spiritual and intellectual pleasure; together they encompass enjoyment beyond creatures’ complete description. Their eternal stay is fact, promise, and glad tiding, yielding incomparable spiritual joy.
verses.72: Al-Mizan reports two readings of inheritance: Paradise is granted because of their deeds, or inherited from faithless people who would have entered it had they believed and acted righteously.
verses.73: Al-Mizan says the mention of abundant fruit completes the enumeration of Paradise’s food and drink. ‘From which’ is partitive and also suggests that its fruit is not exhausted by eating.
verses.74: Al-Mizan says ‘the guilty’ are those habituated to wrongdoing and may include more than unbelievers, since they are contrasted with the more particular Godwary. Their hell-punishment is never eased, and they despair either of God’s mercy or of escape.
verses.75: Al-Mizan says ‘the guilty’ are those habituated to wrongdoing and may include more than unbelievers, since they are contrasted with the more particular Godwary. Their hell-punishment is never eased, and they despair either of God’s mercy or of escape.
verses.76: Al-Mizan says God merely requites their deeds; they wronged themselves by exposing themselves to actions that lead to misery and ruin.
verses.77: Al-Mizan identifies Mālik, in Sunni and Shiʿi reports, as the angel responsible for hell. The inmates address him because they are veiled from God. Their request to be finished off seeks annihilation as escape from torment, reflecting their worldly conception of death as nonexistence, though they have already died and learned otherwise. Mālik’s reply leaves them in their wretched existence and punishment.
verses.78: Al-Mizan prefers this as Mālik’s speech for the angels, since hell’s inmates are cut off from speaking with God, though the alternative is reported. Their aversion to truth belongs to a secondary nature acquired by sin, not their original fiṭrah, which could not ground moral accountability. The verse makes acceptance or rejection of truth the decisive criterion of eternal happiness or misery.
verses.79: Al-Mizan glosses ibrām as tightening and takes the question as their plot against the Prophet. God answers that He too is settling a plan against them, as in (52:42).
verses.80: Al-Mizan says sirr is either concealed thought or a private exchange, and calls God’s knowledge of both ‘hearing’ because the former is inward speech. God hears them, while His messengers are with them recording their deeds.
verses.81: Al-Mizan takes the conditional in as a rhetorically impossible supposition that humbles the claimants: if the All-beneficent had a son, the Prophet would be first to worship him, because a son would share the father’s nature; he does not because he knows no such being exists. It reports, but does not adopt, readings in which he would still worship God alone, in is negation, ʿābidīn means those who disdain, or the phrase is an impossible counterclaim. The apparent meaning remains the first.
verses.82: Al-Mizan says this frees God from their allegations. ‘Lord of the Throne’ explains Lord of heavens and earth: the Throne is His dominion over the perceptible realm. Since creation and governance belong inseparably to Him, His lordship of the Throne proves His lordship and oneness over all.
verses.83: Al-Mizan reads this as a general warning: the Prophet is to leave the faithless absorbed in false talk and play until the promised Day of Resurrection and its punishment.
verses.84: Al-Mizan says God alone is worthy of worship in heaven and on earth; the wording connects both realms to His divinity, not to spatial residence. It counters the claim of separate heavenly and earthly gods. His exclusive wisdom and knowledge also entail exclusive lordship.
verses.85: Al-Mizan treats God’s kingdom of all things, sole knowledge of the Hour, and universal return to Him as proofs of His sole lordship. A governor must know the ultimate destination of what He governs, and the return is for judgment and recompense, the final act of governance; therefore no invoked being besides Him can be Lord.
verses.86: Al-Mizan gives the verse a general scope: every worshipped being besides God lacks intercessory power. The exception is those who know and witness the truth, namely divine unity; knowing the real state and deeds of those for whom they intercede, they intercede only for monotheists whom God approves. The verse thus explicitly affirms shafāʿah.
verses.87: Al-Mizan says their confession that God created them entails that He alone governs them, for tadbīr is inseparable from creation. Their continued turn from this truth of divine unity to idolatry is therefore irrational.
verses.88: Al-Mizan identifies the plaint as the Prophet’s and qīl as a verbal noun. It reports the connection to knowledge of the Hour: God knows his saying, ‘My Lord, these are a people who will not have faith.’
verses.89: Al-Mizan says the Prophet is commanded to disregard them, lose hope of their belief, and say ‘Peace’ as a detached farewell. ‘Soon they will know’ remains a threat; the supposed abrogation by the Sword Verse is dismissed as nonsensical.
